title: The Cap on What Judges Can Earn on the Side
hook: Federal judges may only earn a few tens of thousands of dollars outside the job — a rule meant to keep outside money from buying influence. Writing books is one of the carve-outs.
key_points: Judicial ethics rules cap what a federal judge may earn in outside income each year — roughly $35,000, per SCOTUSblog.
The cap exists so a judge's livelihood cannot quietly depend on anyone with business before the court.
Several categories are excepted from the cap, and writing is one of them — so book royalties are the rare uncapped channel.
Justices' salaries are fixed by law: about $320,700 for the chief justice and $306,600 for associate justices.
Roth reports justices have earned roughly $13 million from books in total, far exceeding what the cap would otherwise allow.
He proposes escrowing book earnings until retirement and creating a Supreme Court ethics officer — a reform argument, not current law.
content_html: Judges are paid a fixed salary set by law, and there is a reason the rules also limit what they can earn anywhere else. If a judge's real income came from outside employers, speaking fees, or consulting, the people paying could gain a quiet hold on someone who is supposed to be beholden to no one. So federal judicial ethics rules cap outside earned income — around $35,000 a year, according to SCOTUSblog — on top of salaries of roughly $320,700 for the chief justice and $306,600 for the associate justices.
extra_html: But the cap carries several exceptions, and writing is one of them. That single carve-out is why book deals have become the one channel through which justices can legally earn sums that dwarf the limit: Gabe Roth, who writes on judicial accountability, reports that the justices have collectively earned about $13 million from books. Roth argues this money deserves the same scrutiny that gifts and travel now receive, and proposes that justices be required to park book earnings in accounts they cannot touch until retirement — with narrow certified exceptions for a home purchase, family medical emergencies, or children's education — overseen by a new Supreme Court ethics officer. That is his reform proposal, not current law; the rules today rely on the cap, its exceptions, and public disclosure. The broader civics point holds regardless of where one lands on the proposal: rules that limit outside income only bind as tightly as their exceptions allow. (This card describes U.S. federal judicial ethics rules specifically.)

related.title: Why Supreme Court Justices Have to Show Their Books
related.hook: Federal judges don't campaign for office or face voters — so how does the public keep tabs on their outside income, gifts, and travel? One tool: a legally required annual disclosure.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: When Judges Step Aside
related.hook: A judge who might be biased is supposed to step aside. But on the U.S. Supreme Court, each justice decides that alone — and no one can overrule them.

flashcards.prompt: Why do ethics rules cap how much a federal judge can earn outside the job?
flashcards.back_html: So that a judge's income cannot come to depend on outside parties — including anyone who might have business before the court — which would create a standing conflict of interest.

flashcards.prompt: Why can justices earn millions from books despite a cap on outside income of roughly $35,000 a year?

choices.text: Writing is one of the categories excepted from the cap
The cap applies only to lower-court judges, not the Supreme Court
Book royalties are legally treated as part of the judicial salary

flashcards.explanation_html: The cap has several exceptions and writing is one of them, which is what makes book deals the one uncapped channel for large outside sums.

flashcards.prompt: What does Gabe Roth propose doing about justices' book earnings?

choices.text: Holding the earnings in accounts justices cannot access until retirement, with limited certified exceptions
Banning justices from writing books at all
Taxing book royalties at the same rate as judicial salaries

flashcards.explanation_html: Roth's proposal is deferral rather than prohibition — plus a Supreme Court ethics officer to certify the narrow exceptions. It is a reform argument, not existing law.
